title: New tool aims to deter gaming in global university rankings
content:
Tweet
Global university rankings risk rewarding visibility over value and quantity over quality, inadvertently incentivising practices that distort the scholarly record and undermine the credibility of academic evaluation – highlighting the need for changes in how scholarly performance is assessed, according to a recent study.
Titled “Gaming the Metrics? Bibliometric Anomalies and the Integrity Crisis in Global University Rankings” , the study examined 18 universities selected from among 98 fast-growing universities for their sharp declines in first and corresponding authorship – an “early warning sign of potential metric manipulation”.
The 18 universities were from India (7), Lebanon (1), Saudi Arabia (9) and the United Arab Emirates (1).
The study, which has not been peer-reviewed, was published in the open-access bioRxiv archive, the preprint server for biology, on 19 June. It aimed to explore how global university rankings “incentivise institutions to prioritise bibliometric indicators at the expense of research integrity”.
The study argued that “the magnitude and speed of publication growth among the 18 universities, often exceeding 400% within five years, raise questions about whether such expansion can be attributed to organic academic development alone”.
It suggests that while publication surges and citation gains among the universities might reflect growing research capacity or internationalisation, the accompanying “decline in first and corresponding authorship roles, increased reliance on delisted journals, dense reciprocal collaboration and citation networks, and rising retraction rates suggest that more complex and potentially problematic dynamics are at play”.
It suggests further that the “anomalous bibliometric patterns, concentration in STEM fields, and absence of similar gains in disciplines such as clinical medicine and the social sciences … suggest more strategic, ranking-orientated expansion” and a “deliberate focus on maximising bibliometric output”.
Research Integrity Risk Index
To assess these risks globally, the author developed the Research Integrity Risk Index (RI²), a composite profiling metric combining retraction rates and reliance on delisted journals into a single score and ranking.
The index aims to identify institutions with atypical global research performance patterns, highlighting systemic vulnerabilities in current evaluation frameworks and underscoring the need to “rethink how research performance is measured to safeguard academic integrity and mitigate gaming behaviours”.
Study author Professor Lokman Meho, based at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, said the aim of the study was not to “accuse specific institutions” but to spark a conversation about how global ranking systems may inadvertently incentivise practices that compromise research integrity.
“The study reveals how the gaming of research metrics is distorting global academia, undermining research integrity, and creating an uneven playing field in which ethical researchers and institutions are forced to compete against artificially inflated benchmarks,” Meho told University World News.
Describing his RI² as an “empirically grounded, conservative tool that flags institutions exhibiting structural integrity risks based on retraction rates and reliance on delisted journals”, he said, rather than a punitive tool, the index offers institutions a chance to detect integrity risks before they become reputational liabilities.
“RI² helps institutions and policymakers detect and monitor such risks early, encouraging more responsible, integrity-sensitive research practices and institutional benchmarking,” Meho said.
“RI² helps shift the focus from sheer volume and visibility to structural signals of ethical risk, offering universities a path towards more sustainable and transparent academic performance,” he said, adding: “Its reliance on existing public data ensures it can be adopted globally without costly infrastructure changes.”
Meaningful scholarship Meho said for higher education policymakers, the study underscores the need to balance the pursuit of global visibility with the preservation of academic integrity. “While rankings and performance indicators can drive progress, they must not incentivise behaviours that compromise ethical research practices. Sustainable academic prestige stems from meaningful scholarship, not inflated numbers." He said for decision-makers in the examined institutions, the findings are a “wake-up call for urgent reform”. “In many cases, institutional strategies, whether explicit or tacit, appear to encourage practices that inflate research output at the expense of credibility. These [university] leaders must re-examine their incentive structures, recruitment practices, and international partnerships to ensure long-term academic values are not sacrificed for short-term reputational gain.” He said this included implementing transparent authorship audits, enforcing consequences for misconduct, and investing in a rigorous, mentorship-driven research culture. “Ultimately, the focus must shift from metric optimisation to sustainable capacity-building,” Meho said. Meho told University World News he believed global university rankings should evolve to incorporate integrity-sensitive, risk-adjusted indicators such as retraction rates, publication in delisted journals, and patterns of hyper-prolific or ethically questionable authorship. “These indicators help differentiate genuine academic performance from metric-driven inflation,” he said. “Ranking agencies should also commit to greater transparency in their methodologies and data sources and actively collaborate with independent bibliometric experts to refine evaluation frameworks that prioritise responsible and ethical scholarship over sheer volume or citation counts,” Meho noted. Rankings should also introduce and disclose penalties for verified cases of misconduct or systemic integrity risks, including conditional inclusion, integrity-adjustment factors, or public reporting, Meho suggested, adding that tools such as RI² could fill this gap in the interim, offering independent oversight, even when formal accountability mechanisms were lacking. Challenges of integrity-sensitive reform However, he conceded that the implementation of integrity-sensitive reforms in university rankings faced several challenges. “First, while retraction rates and the share of publications in delisted journals are reliable and quantifiable indicators of integrity risk, it is more difficult to develop and apply broader integrity measures consistently at a global level,” he said. This difficulty, he argued, stems from a lack of consensus on how to define and quantify other forms of questionable research practices, such as guest or sole authorship, excessive self-citation, or citation cartels. “Second, there is the risk of metric substitution, where institutions adjust their behaviour to game integrity metrics as they have done with traditional indicators,” he said. “Third, commercial incentives may make ranking providers reluctant to adopt reforms that disrupt established hierarchies or challenge popular perceptions. Universities benefiting from current methodologies may also resist changes that lower their positions or disrupt internal reward systems,” he said. He said the strength of RI² was that it did not rely on institutional self-reporting, cooperation, or disclosure but used bibliometric data that were publicly available and verifiable. “This makes RI² uniquely positioned to function independently and offer actionable integrity monitoring even in the absence of formal consensus or policy change,” Meho said. He suggested the academic community prioritise concrete, incremental steps that are feasible with current tools and data. “For example, institutions and ranking providers can begin using RI² alongside traditional metrics to identify red flags and validate assessments without requiring structural overhauls. “Ranking providers should be encouraged to share raw data, including publication counts, collaboration patterns, and citation sources, to allow independent replication and scrutiny,” Meho noted. He suggested that databases such as Retraction Watch be integrated into bibliometric workflows, and ORCID verification should be mandated for authorship attribution and evaluation. “Governments and funders should tie research funding to basic integrity thresholds or disclosures, such as authorship audits and absence of unresolved misconduct investigations. “Universities, in turn, should institutionalise regular authorship audits, promote ethical research training, and use RI² to monitor and reduce their exposure to integrity risks. “Reform will take time, but the stakes of preserving public trust in science and ensuring fair recognition for rigorous research are too high to ignore,” Meho said. A ‘promising tool’ Dr Mini Agrawal, based at Amity Business School in India, told University World News that Meho’s study offered “timely and credible” insights and drew particular attention to the finding that seven Indian universities in the study had recorded publication growth of up to 766%, compared to a national average of 50%. “The RI² index is a promising tool for identifying integrity risks and fostering responsible research. I support the call for reforms that balance performance metrics with ethical safeguards to uphold academic credibility,” Agrawal said. Higher education global expert Angel Calderon, director of strategic insights at RMIT University in Australia, said the development of the Research Integrity Risk Index was a “novel initiative”, which should help institutions and the wider academic community identify instances where malpractice occurs. “I believe the index is a useful accountability tool,” Calderon said, adding: “The index should also assist the worldwide publishing companies such as Elsevier and Clarivate to maintain quality and integrity with their extensive collections.” “The findings of Meho’s study may also help global rankers spot instances of unusual publication and citation patterns. It may be pertinent that the various World University Rankings introduce a metric that identifies institutions that have a clear research integrity and ethics process in place,” Calderon said. Dr Elizabeth Gadd, head of Research Culture and Assessment at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom, told University World News the poor incentives provided by publication-dominant global university rankings were “well documented". “What is less common are concrete solutions for tackling the problem,” said Gadd, who also serves as a vice-chair of the Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment. “While innovations like RI² may disincentivise publication-related gaming, ideally we’d be seeking better forms of university assessment that were less publication-dominant in the first place, instead valuing the broader range of contributions that universities make to society and scholarship," Gadd said. Who should police the sector? Duncan Ross , former chief data officer of the Times Higher Education (THE), told University World News: “I think that there is an overemphasis on the importance of rankings and an under-recognition of the internal factors that make academics want to publish more articles. “After all, universities do not publish; academics do,” Ross said. “By far the greatest driver is likely to be the internal and external recognition brought on by publications (without sufficient publications an academic will not be promoted-invited to present, etcetera). “In practice, rankings organisations have already looked at how to adjust for the raw number of articles, with measures that are more nuanced than [are] suggested here [in Meho’s study],” Ross said. “THE and QS World University Rankings both use Elsevier’s Scopus database and exclude ‘suspended’ journals. “It is not reasonable to expect rankings organisations to police the higher education sector. That is something that the higher education sector itself should do,” Ross noted. University World News reached out to QS and THE World University Rankings for their views on the study’s findings and recommendations but received no response.

title: Higher education: How (not) to cope with a deficit
content:
Tweet
A shockingly large number of universities worldwide seem to be approaching a state of financial distress. Budget deficits are spiralling, triggering staff redundancy programmes, department shutdowns and the mothballing of degree programmes, among other measures.
Universities in the United Kingdom are the most prominent example. Suppose current trends continue and no corrective action is taken. In that case, the UK Office for Students projects that 72% of UK universities will run a deficit by 2025 to 2026, amounting to £1.636 billion (US$2.24 billion) for the sector. As many as 40% will see their liquidity reserves dwindle to cover less than 30 days cash on hand.
Even Russell Group institutions are affected, as demonstrated by the case of the University of Edinburgh. It recently announced a cost-cutting programme of £140 million and 350 voluntary redundancies. Other examples include Cardiff University, Durham University, King’s College London and the universities of Sheffield and Nottingham.
A brief postmortem
But how effective are crisis management practices in creating a financially sustainable, strategy-informed future? In our view, there is much to be criticised. Resorting to these appears to be the equivalent of delaying cancer treatment until the patient has reached stage 4 and then using a broad-band, low-efficacy drug as a cure.
To address how universities can better cope with a structural deficit, we will first conduct a brief postmortem of what led universities to their current state and then offer concrete, actionable alternatives to current practices.
Contributing factors to the current state of affairs include the decline in international tuition revenues resulting from tightened immigration policies in prominent receiving countries, as well as widening gaps between cost inflation and income growth.
However, the writing has been on the wall for a long time, with under-managed cluster risks in international student recruitment and over-investment in ‘commercially unproductive’ faculty research capacities, both of which lead to a margin squeeze in times of distress.
Intra-university cross-subsidisation schemes and thin financial reserves at the university level exacerbate the pressure on professional schools to continue meeting ambitious revenue targets.
Furthermore, many universities have over-leveraged themselves with physical infrastructure investments based on overly optimistic growth projections.
Fragile universities may find restructuring to be a challenging and sometimes insurmountable task. Financial distress is often accompanied by leadership turnover and interim appointments, suggesting a lack of experience in crisis management.
That may explain the indiscriminate roll-out of countermeasures, such as reductions in staff costs through voluntary and involuntary redundancies, affecting both senior and junior staff, as well as the freezing of staff recruitment and promotions.
Cuts in discretionary budgets (for example, to fund faculty research) and temporary increases in teaching loads for faculty who stay are often part of the mix as well. This raises the question of how a significant workforce reduction (for example, 7% at Cardiff University) affects an institution’s ability to shape its future.
If one allows a crisis to shift from a strategic to a financial one, the emergency crew must be dispatched to stop the bleeding of cash flow. However, this typically involves broad strokes, prioritising speed of action over strategically informed resource planning.
This approach is operationally disruptive and can undermine the organisational fabric necessary for moving forward. It can also trigger a downward spiral of continuously haemorrhaging the personnel talent needed to build the university’s future.
A five-step plan
We propose a five-step approach as an alternative pathway to addressing short-term restructuring needs while fostering the creation of a more agile and resilient organisation.
• Diversifying revenue sources should ultimately be the top priority for schools and universities navigating financial distress. Strategically tapping into alternative income streams, such as executive education, online learning platforms and consulting, has become essential for funding restructuring programmes and future-orientated investments.
However, hasty investments in new commercial ventures should be avoided, as they are often poorly conceived and tend to result in negative financial returns. The acquisition of equity capital, for example, from engaged alumni and corporate sponsors, offers another vital channel. Alumni investors may be willing to compromise on dividend and control rights and may also agree to a finite maturity.
• Financial distress presents an opportunity for the university to deconstruct its administration, making it more project-driven, technology-focused and data-driven, ultimately freeing up financial resources.
While typically operated top-down, university structures often resemble a collection of siloed, bureaucratic clusters that generate vested interests and resistance to change. Integrating these clusters is crucial to achieving unity of purpose in the transformation journey, with cost efficiency gains to be realised along the way.
• Making educational offerings scalable and flexible is often a key step towards economic recovery. For example, it involves eliminating inefficient stand-alone operations, interlinking degree programmes and in-degree study pathways, and using digital platforms to expand serviceable markets.
Degree offerings can be unbundled into stackable learning opportunities, gradually easing learners into formally registering for the programme. Instead of using annual and fundamental programme reviews to guide curricular, pedagogical and assessment reforms, they should become a continuous improvement process to ensure currentness.
• Universities should reconsider their approach to delivering an educational service from beginning to end, especially if it also involves the deployment of efficiency-enhancing technologies. For example, the semi-automation of candidate selection and admissions processes using AI holds great potential, especially in the context of international student recruitment. This also presents an opportunity to optimise organisational structures and processes, thereby improving coordination and eliminating bottlenecks that hinder effective and timely decision-making. • Last, but not least, universities need to urgently professionalise their risk management processes, especially those that are already in distress. The commonly used risk registers have many flaws, including a failure to capture risk interdependencies and the use of subjective metrics to assess likelihood and impact, which necessitates complementing them with more sophisticated analytics. More attention needs to be given to how to position the university to benefit from unanticipated developments. This brings us back to the concept of agility and resilience. Universities must be redesigned to react flexibly to shocks. Being able to respond faster and more easily than competitors will make all the difference. In sum, universities should adopt a more flexible approach by loosening their ties to established plans and administrative principles while embracing a trial-and-error mindset. The future will show whether the monolithic, traditional and currently struggling universities will find a turnaround and regain their competitive dominance. Wolfram Berger is a professor of economics at Brandenburg University of Technology, Germany, and an executive consultant at XOLAS Advisors GmbH, a Germany-based higher education consultancy.
